name: Infosys (SE, DSE, Specialist Programmer)
tagline: From System Engineer to Specialist Programmer and Power Programmer

overview.about: Infosys hires freshers mainly as System Engineer (SE), Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE) and Specialist Programmer (SP). Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.

HackWithInfy is open to engineering students of the batches announced for that edition

cards.title: Three main fresher roles

cards.title: SE test sections
cards.body: Logical reasoning, mathematical ability, verbal ability, pseudo-code and puzzle solving, each with sectional timing. Pattern as reported for 2025–26 drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Mathematical ability is the filter
cards.body: Infosys maths is a notch above typical service-company quant: number theory, P&C, probability, geometry and functions. Practise accuracy over speed.

cards.title: Sample: mathematical ability
cards.body:
Q: How many positive divisors does 360 have?
360 = 2³ × 3² × 5 → (3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 24.

cards.title: Sample: pseudo-code
cards.body:
x = 0
for i = 1 to 10
  if i mod 3 == 0: x = x + i
print x
→ 3 + 6 + 9 = 18

cards.title: Puzzle solving
cards.body: Logic grids, arrangement puzzles and 'who is lying' questions. Draw a table; eliminate impossible cells first.

cards.q:
s = 1
for i = 1 to 4
  s = s * i
print s — output?

notes.h: Roles you can be hired for
notes.p:
Infosys hires freshers mainly as **Systems Engineer (SE)**, with higher-paying roles such as **Digital Specialist Engineer (DSE)** and **Specialist Programmer (SP)** for candidates who show stronger coding skills. Role names, packages and eligibility change between drives. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

Routes include the on-campus/off-campus **online test** for SE, and coding-focused routes (including **HackWithInfy** and dedicated DSE/SP coding rounds) for higher roles.

Recent SE tests are reported to contain these sections, each timed separately: **Reasoning Ability**, **Mathematical Ability**, **Verbal Ability**, **Pseudo-code** and **Puzzle Solving**. The math section is known to be harder than at most service companies, while verbal is fast-paced. Cut-offs may apply per section, so do not ignore any part.
points: Reasoning: arrangements, data sufficiency, syllogisms, blood relations, coding-decoding.
Math: number system, permutations/probability, geometry, algebra, time-work.
Verbal: grammar, sentence correction, RC, para-jumbles, vocabulary.
Pseudo-code: output tracing, loops, recursion, bitwise operators.
Puzzles: logic puzzles, mathematical patterns, visual reasoning.

notes.p:
**Math.** How many ways can 5 boys and 3 girls sit in a row so that no two girls are together? Arrange boys: 5! = 120. Gaps around them: 6. Choose and arrange girls in gaps: 6P3 = 120. Total = **14,400**.

**Pseudo-code.** `x = 1; for i = 1 to 4: x = x * 2 + i; print x`. Trace: 3, 8, 19, 42 → **42**.

**Puzzle.** If 5 machines make 5 widgets in 5 minutes, how long do 100 machines take for 100 widgets? Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes → **5 minutes**.

**Reasoning.** Data sufficiency: 'Is P the tallest of P, Q, R?' (1) P > Q (2) R < Q. Together: P > Q > R → **both together are sufficient**, neither alone.

`from math import factorial, perm
print(factorial(5) * perm(6, 3))
x = 1
for i in range(1, 5):
    x = x * 2 + i
print(x)`

Output:
`14400
42`

points: Attempt math with full focus; it carries the biggest risk.
In verbal, answer quickly and do not overthink grammar questions.
For pseudo-code, use a trace table on rough paper.
For puzzles, read twice and write the constraints.
Practise past-pattern mocks, including on InfyTQ/Infosys Springboard resources where available.

notes.p: Where candidates commonly slip in the Infosys test:
points: Spending too long on one hard math question and running out of time for easier ones.
Ignoring a section because it 'carries fewer questions' — sectional cut-offs can still eliminate you.
In pseudo-code, assuming integer division behaves like real division.
In puzzles, missing a constraint hidden in the last line.
Applying with incorrect academic details — they are verified later.
Roles: SE (base), DSE and SP (coding-heavy, higher pay).
Five timed sections; possible sectional cut-offs.
Math section is the toughest — practise P&C and number system.
Trace pseudo-code line by line.
Puzzles reward careful reading.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Format
cards.body: As reported: 3 problems in about 3 hours — usually one easy, one medium and one hard. Partial scores per test case. Cut-offs apply, so the easy problem must be fully solved.

cards.title: Common topics
points: Greedy and sorting
Dynamic programming (subsequence, knapsack, grid DP)
Graphs: BFS/DFS, shortest paths
Strings, bit manipulation, binary search on the answer

cards.title: HackWithInfy
cards.body: Infosys's national coding contest for engineering students. Top performers get interview opportunities for SP/Power Programmer roles plus prizes. Registration is announced on the Infosys careers site.

cards.title: Sample-style problem
cards.body:
Given n tasks with deadlines and profits, schedule one task per unit time to maximise profit.
Idea: sort by profit (desc), place each task in the latest free slot ≤ its deadline (greedy, O(n log n) with DSU).

cards.title: Partial marks matter
cards.body: If the hard problem is out of reach, write a brute force that passes small test cases. Every passed test case counts.

cards.title: Preparation plan
cards.body: Solve ~100 medium and ~30 hard problems across DP, graphs and greedy on a free judge, timing yourself to 45 minutes per medium problem.

cards.q: In a 3-problem, 3-hour coding test, the best opening move is usually:
options: Fully solve the easiest problem first
Write all three solutions without testing
cards.explain: Securing the easy problem clears cut-offs and builds time for the rest.

cards.q: Job sequencing with deadlines is typically solved by:
options: Greedy: sort by profit, fill latest free slot
cards.explain: Taking the most profitable jobs first and scheduling them as late as possible is optimal.

notes.p:
**HackWithInfy** is Infosys's national coding contest for engineering students. Top performers have been offered interviews for **SP** and **DSE** roles (and pre-placement interview opportunities). Contest rounds are reported to give **3 problems in about 3 hours**, from medium to hard (greedy, DP, graphs, number theory). Separately, DSE/SP hiring drives run their own coding rounds with similar difficulty. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

Scoring usually depends on **test cases passed**, so a correct brute-force solution that passes small cases still earns partial marks. Write the simple solution first, submit, then optimise.

notes.h: Sample problem: maximum sum of non-adjacent elements
notes.p:
**Problem.** Given n house values, choose houses to maximise the total such that no two chosen houses are next to each other.

**Idea (DP).** For each house, best = max(skip it → best up to previous house, take it → best up to two houses back + value). Only two variables are needed.

`n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
take, skip = 0, 0
for x in a:
    take, skip = skip + x, max(take, skip)
print(max(take, skip))`

Sample input:
`5
2 7 9 3 1`

Output:
`12`

Chosen houses: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12. Time **O(n)**, space **O(1)**. A brute force over all subsets would be O(2ⁿ).

notes.h: Sample problem: count subarrays with sum K
notes.p:
**Problem.** Count contiguous subarrays whose sum is exactly K (values may be negative).

`from collections import defaultdict

n, k = map(int, input().split())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))
seen = defaultdict(int)
seen[0] = 1
total = count = 0
for x in a:
    total += x
    count += seen[total - k]
    seen[total] += 1
print(count)`

Sample input:
`5 2
1 1 1 0 1`

Output:
`4`

Prefix sums: a subarray (i, j] sums to K exactly when prefix[j] − prefix[i] = K. Counting earlier prefixes in a hash map gives **O(n)** time instead of O(n²).
A focused plan for Infosys coding rounds:
points: Master arrays, strings, hashing, sorting, binary search, two pointers.
Then DP (knapsack, LIS, grid paths), greedy, BFS/DFS, basic number theory (gcd, modular arithmetic, sieve).
Practise on contest platforms under time limits.
Always check constraints: n ≤ 10⁵ needs O(n log n) or better.
Use 64-bit integers in C++/Java when sums can be large; take answers modulo 10⁹ + 7 when asked.

notes.p:
**Q: Do I need competitive programming to get SE?** A: No. SE relies on the aptitude-style online test; strong coding helps for DSE/SP.

**Q: Which language should I use?** A: The one you are fastest and most accurate in. C++ and Java are fast; Python is quicker to write but may be slower on very large inputs.

**Q: What if I cannot find the optimal solution?** A: Submit a correct brute force for partial marks, then try to optimise with sorting, hashing or DP.

points: HackWithInfy → SP/DSE interview opportunities.
Partial scoring by test cases: submit brute force first.
Read constraints to choose complexity.
Prefix sums + hash map for subarray-sum counts.
DP with two variables for non-adjacent selection.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

cards.title: Technical interview (SE)
cards.body: Basics of one language, OOP, DBMS queries, simple programs (prime, palindrome, Fibonacci), and your project. Clarity matters more than breadth.

cards.title: Technical interview (DSE/SP)
cards.body: Live DSA problem-solving with complexity analysis, follow-ups on your coding-round solution, CS fundamentals in depth and sometimes basic system design.

cards.title: HR round
cards.body: Self-introduction, relocation readiness, interest in Infosys, strengths and weaknesses. Keep answers honest and concise.

cards.title: Training at Mysuru
cards.body: Selected freshers usually go through foundation training at the Infosys Global Education Centre, Mysuru, followed by assessments. Taking training seriously matters for project allocation.

cards.title: Explain your coding-round solution
cards.body: Interviewers often open your test submission. Be ready to explain your approach, its complexity and how you'd improve it.

cards.title: Common SE question
cards.body: "Write a program to check whether a string is a palindrome without using reverse()." → two pointers from both ends; mention O(n) time, O(1) space.

cards.q: For a DSE/SP interview, which preparation is most important?
options: DSA problem solving with complexity analysis

cards.q: Time complexity of the two-pointer palindrome check:
cards.explain: Each character is compared at most once.

notes.p: After clearing the test, candidates usually face a **technical interview** and an **HR interview** (sometimes combined, 20–45 minutes). For SE, questions focus on fundamentals and your project; for DSE/SP, expect live coding and deeper DSA and system questions. Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.

**Q: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?** A: An abstract class can have state and constructors and supports single inheritance; an interface defines a contract and a class can implement many.

**Q: Write a program to check if a string is a palindrome.** A: Compare characters from both ends moving inward, or compare the string with its reverse; O(n).

**Q: What is normalisation? Why is it needed?** A: Organising tables to reduce redundancy and update anomalies, using normal forms such as 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.

**Q: Explain the difference between a process and a thread.** A: A process has its own memory; threads within a process share memory and are cheaper to switch.

**Q: What happens when you type a URL in the browser?** A: DNS lookup, TCP (and TLS) handshake, HTTP request, server response, rendering.

**Q (SP/DSE): Find the longest substring without repeating characters.** A: Sliding window with a last-seen map; O(n).

**Q: Why Infosys?** A: Mention specific points such as its structured training for freshers, its scale of client projects, and its focus on digital services, then connect to your goals.

**Q: Are you willing to relocate?** A: Answer honestly; postings can be anywhere in India.

**Q: What do you know about Infosys?** A: Founded in 1981, headquartered in Bengaluru, a large global IT services and consulting company. Keep facts accurate and current from the official site.

**Q: Tell me about a time you learned something quickly.** A: Use STAR: situation, task, your actions, measurable result.

Infosys is known for its **foundation training programme** for freshers, historically at its **Mysuru** campus (format can be on-campus or online by batch). Training covers programming, databases, web technologies and soft skills, and includes **assessments** that must be cleared. Taking training seriously matters: performance can affect your stream and project allocation. Confirm current details in your offer documents.

points: Revise OOP, DBMS, OS, networks and one programming language thoroughly.
Practise writing small programs on paper or a shared editor without autocomplete.
Prepare a 2-minute project explanation and be ready for 'what would you improve?'.
Read the company's latest annual report highlights for HR questions.
Keep documents (marksheets, ID) ready for verification.
Technical + HR, sometimes combined.
SE: fundamentals + project; DSE/SP: live coding + DSA.
Know URL flow, OOP, normalisation, process vs thread.
Give specific reasons for choosing Infosys.
Training includes assessments you must clear.
Pattern as reported for recent drives; confirm on the official careers page.
